analysis.investment_thesis: Jamna Auto is India's dominant leaf spring manufacturer (~68% CV market share) with a 70-year operating history and lean balance sheet — a quality niche business, but a thoroughly cyclical one priced at 25x earnings during a revenue downturn (FY25 revenue -6.5%, profit -12% YoY). Wait for a better entry or clearer CV cycle recovery before adding capital.
key_strengths: Market leadership with ~68% share in commercial vehicle leaf springs — genuine pricing power in a narrow niche
Near debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.15, net cash ~0 after netting 140 Cr cash vs 140 Cr total debt) with ROCE of 20.7%
Disciplined deleveraging — finance costs collapsed from 20 Cr (2016) to 5 Cr (2025), showing capital discipline
key_risks: Classic cyclical business — FY2020 saw revenue crash 47% (2,135→1,129 Cr); FY2025 already showing renewed decline
Rising capex cycle (196 Cr in FY25, CWIP surged to 270 Cr) risks return dilution if CV demand stays soft
Structural EV transition risk for CVs long-term could erode leaf spring demand, though timeline is uncertain
red_flags: FCF/Net Income of only 57% in FY25 (103/180 Cr) — below Munger's 80% quality threshold, partly capex-driven but bears watching
FY2025 revenue and profit both declining YoY despite India infrastructure tailwinds — suggests CV demand weakness not fully priced in at 25x P/E
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Inversion first: what makes this dangerous? Jamna Auto earns its returns almost entirely from one product (leaf springs) sold to one sector (commercial vehicles). The FY2020 episode — revenue halved, net profit collapsed 65% to 48 Cr — is the honest base case stress test. We are now seeing a mild repeat: FY25 revenue fell to 2,270 Cr from 2,427 Cr, net profit to 180 from 205 Cr. Paying 25x earnings for a cyclical at the top of an earnings curve is precisely the mistake Munger warns against. That said, the business itself is genuinely good: 20.7% ROCE, expanding reserves (477→996 Cr in five years), near-zero debt, and a customer base that cannot easily substitute a dominant supplier mid-cycle.

The heavy capex cycle (163 Cr FY24, 196 Cr FY25, CWIP at 270 Cr) is the critical near-term variable. If this is capacity addition for air suspension, lift axles, and stabilizer bars — higher-margin, growing adjacencies — it could re-rate the business upward. If the CV cycle stays depressed, these assets will sit underutilized and drag ROIC below the 15% threshold. Forward P/E of 19.5x assumes earnings recovery; that is a reasonable bet but not a margin-of-safety bet. At INR 95–105 (roughly 15x normalized earnings of ~200 Cr), this becomes genuinely interesting. At 129, it is fair but not compelling — a business worth understanding deeply and owning at the right price.
